text: Pluto, designated as minor-planet 134340, is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond Neptune's orbit. It is the ninth-largest and tenth-most-massive known object directly orbiting the Sun, the largest known trans-Neptunian object by volume, though less massive than Eris. Composed primarily of ice and rock, Pluto is much smaller than the inner planets and has roughly one-sixth the mass and one-third the volume of the Moon. Originally classified as a planet, its status changed when the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in 2006 adopted a new definition of planet that excluded dwarf planets like Pluto. Pluto has a moderately eccentric and inclined orbit, ranging from 30 to 49 astronomical units (4.5 to 7.3 billion kilometers; 2.8 to 4.6 billion miles) from the Sun, with light from the Sun taking 5.5 hours to reach it at its average distance of 39.5 AU (5.91 billion km; 3.67 billion mi). Despite occasionally being closer to the Sun than Neptune, a stable orbital resonance prevents collision. Pluto has five known moons: Charon, the largest with a diameter just over half that of Pluto; Styx; Nix; Kerberos; and Hydra. Pluto and Charon are considered a binary system because their barycenter lies outside both bodies, and they are tidally locked. The New Horizons spacecraft made the first flyby of Pluto and its moons on July 14, 2015, taking detailed measurements and observations. Discovered in 1930 by Clyde W. Tombaugh at the Lowell Observatory, Pluto was initially hailed as the ninth planet. Doubts arose due to its small size, especially after the discovery of Eris in 2005, a more massive scattered disk object. In 2006, the IAU formally redefined a planet, requiring an object to orbit the Sun, be spherical, and have cleared its orbit of other debris—conditions Pluto fails to meet, as its mass is only 0.07 times that of the combined mass of other objects in its orbit. The IAU classified Pluto, Eris, and Eris's moon Dysnomia as dwarf planets, assigning them minor-planet designations (134340) Pluto, (136199) Eris, and (136199) Eris I Dysnomia. The name Pluto, derived from the Roman god of the underworld and an epithet for Hades, was proposed by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, and selected by a vote at the Lowell Observatory, which unanimously approved it. The name was published on May 1, 1930. The symbol for Pluto, a monogram of "PL," was created at the time but is rarely used in astronomy, though common in astrology. The name inspired Mickey Mouse's dog, Pluto, and the element plutonium, named by Glenn T. Seaborg in 1940. Most languages use "Pluto," with Japanese, Chinese, and Korean adopting Meiōsei (冥王星), while Hindi and other Indian languages use Yama, the Hindu god of death. Polynesian languages use indigenous underworld deities, such as Māori Whiro. Vietnamese uses Yama as Sao Diêm Vương due to phonological constraints. Early estimates of Pluto's mass were high—initially thought to be Earth-sized in 1931, then Mars-sized in 1948—before being revised to 0.2% of Earth's mass in 1978 after the discovery of Charon, which allowed accurate mass measurement. This mass was too small to explain orbital discrepancies in Uranus, which were later resolved by updated Neptune mass estimates from Voyager 2 data in 1992. By 2000, most scientists agreed that Lowell's Planet X did not exist, though his 1915 prediction was close to Pluto's actual orbit, a coincidence noted by Ernest W. Brown. The discovery of numerous Kuiper belt objects, including those as large as Pluto, intensified debate over its planetary status. In 1998, Brian G. Marsden suggested assigning Pluto minor-planet number 10000 while retaining its planetary status, prompting public outcry and the IAU clarifying it was not proposing removal. In 2005, the discovery of Eris, more massive than Pluto, intensified the debate, with many viewing it as a strong argument for reclassifying Pluto. At the 2006 IAU triennial meeting, astronomers Julio Ángel Fernández and Gonzalo Tancredi proposed the three criteria for planetary status, which Pluto fails due to not clearing its orbit. The IAU's decision faced resistance from planetary scientists, including Alan Stern and Marc W. Buie, who rejected it, while some, like Mike Brown, supported it. Public reaction was mixed, with a California Assembly resolution calling the decision a "scientific heresy" and New Mexico and Illinois passing resolutions honoring Clyde Tombaugh and affirming Pluto's planetary status. The American Dialect Society named "plutoed" word of the year in 2006, defining it as to demote or devalue. In April 2024, Arizona passed a law designating Pluto as the official state planet. In 2008, a conference at Johns Hopkins titled "The Great Planet Debate" concluded that scientists could not reach consensus on the definition of a planet. The IAU later introduced the term "plutoid" for Pluto-like objects beyond Neptune, though it has not gained widespread use. Pluto's orbital period is about 248 years, with a significant inclination of over 17° and moderate eccentricity, placing it in a region occasionally closer to the Sun than Neptune. The Pluto–Charon barycenter reached perihelion on September 5, 1989.

Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory hosted a conference titled "The Great Planet Debate" that featured back-to-back talks on the IAU definition of a planet, concluding with a post-conference press release stating that scientists could not reach a consensus on the definition. In June 2008, the IAU announced the term "plutoid" to describe Pluto and other planetary-mass objects with an orbital semi-major axis greater than Neptune’s, though this term has not seen significant use. Pluto’s orbital period is approximately 248 years, with a moderately inclined orbit (over 17°) relative to the ecliptic and moderately eccentric (elliptical), meaning a small portion of its orbit lies closer to the Sun than Neptune’s. The Pluto–Charon barycenter reached perihelion on September 5, 1989, and was last closer to the Sun than Neptune between February 7, 1979, and February 11, 1999. Despite the 2:3 resonance with Neptune, Pluto’s inclination and eccentricity behave chaotically, and computer simulations can only reliably predict its position for up to about 10–20 million years due to sensitivity to immeasurably small Solar System details. Pluto’s semi-major axis varies between 39.3 and 39.6 AU with a 19,951-year period, corresponding to an orbital period between 246 and 249 years, and this is currently increasing. Although Pluto’s orbit appears to cross Neptune’s when viewed from certain angles, the two bodies do not intersect; Pluto passes about 8 AU north of Neptune’s orbit, preventing a collision. This is further protected by the 2:3 orbital resonance: for every two orbits Pluto completes, Neptune completes three, in a rotating frame where Pluto’s perihelion precesses at about 0.97×10−4 degrees per year, with each cycle lasting about 495 years. When Pluto is at perihelion, Neptune is initially 57° ahead, and by the second perihelion, Neptune is 123° behind, resulting in a minimum separation of over 17 AU—greater than Pluto’s minimum distance from Uranus. This resonance is highly stable and has persisted over millions of years, preventing any close approach. When Pluto’s orbital period slightly deviates from 3/2 of Neptune’s, its distance from Neptune drifts; near perihelion, it moves interior to Neptune’s orbit and approaches from behind, remaining between 50° and 65° behind Neptune for about 100 years (e.g., 1937–2036). Gravitational interactions transfer angular momentum to Pluto, increasing its orbital radius and period, and after several cycles, the system returns to a stable state over about 20,000 years. Numerical studies show that the general alignment between Pluto and Neptune’s orbits remains unchanged over millions of years, with additional stability from two mechanisms: first, Pluto’s argument of perihelion librates around 90°, meaning it is farthest north when closest to the Sun, preventing encounters with Neptune; the amplitude of this libration is 38°, so the angular separation between Pluto’s perihelion and Neptune’s orbit is always greater than 52°, with the closest separation occurring every 10,000 years. Second, the longitudes of ascending nodes of Pluto and Neptune are in near-resonance, forming a 1:1 superresonance when aligned, placing Pluto’s perihelion at 90° and ensuring it is farthest north when closest to the Sun; this superresonance is influenced by all four Jovian planets. Pluto’s rotation period is 6.387 Earth days, with an axial tilt of 120°, causing extreme seasonal variation—where one-fourth of its surface experiences continuous daylight and another fourth continuous darkness at solstices. Research from the University of Arizona suggests this tilt results from polar wander due to the buildup of frozen nitrogen in shadowed areas, caused by temperatures as low as −240 °C (33.1 K) at the equator, which leads to nitrogen freezing. This polar wandering effect would be observable on Earth if the Antarctic ice sheet were much larger. Pluto’s surface is composed of over 98% nitrogen ice, with traces of methane and carbon monoxide; nitrogen and carbon monoxide are most abundant on the anti-Charon face (around 180° longitude, including Sputnik Planitia), while methane is most abundant near 300° east; mountains are made of water ice. The surface shows large variations in brightness and color, ranging from charcoal black to dark orange and white, with notable features including Tombaugh Regio ("Heart"), Belton Regio ("Whale"), and the "Brass Knuckles." Sputnik Planitia, a 1,000 km-wide basin of frozen nitrogen and carbon monoxide, features polygonal cells interpreted as convection cells, sublimation pits, and glacial flows, with no visible craters to New Horizons, indicating a surface younger than 10 million years—recent studies estimate its age at 180,000±90,000−40,000 years. The New Horizons team described Pluto as displaying a wide variety of geological landforms, including those from glacial and surface-atmosphere interactions, impacts, tectonics, possible cryovolcanism, and mass-wasting. In western Sputnik Planitia, transverse dunes formed by winds from the basin to surrounding mountains have wavelengths of 0.4–1 km and consist of methane particles 200–300 μm in size. Pluto’s density is 1.853±0.004 g/cm³, and scientists expect its internal structure to be differentiated, with a rocky core (pre-New Horizons estimate: 1700 km in diameter, 70% of Pluto’s diameter) surrounded by a water-ice mantle. Evidence suggests a subsurface ocean of liquid water 100 to 180 km thick at the core–mantle boundary, supported by Brown University simulations in September 2016 showing liquid water upwelling after a collision that formed Sputnik Planitia. In June 2020, astronomers reported evidence that Pluto may have had a subsurface ocean and could have been habitable when first formed; in March 2022, researchers proposed that Wright Mons and Piccard Mons are mergers of smaller cryovolcanic domes, indicating previously unanticipated internal heat. Pluto’s diameter is 2,376.6±3.2 km and its mass is (1.303±0.003)×10²² kg, which is 17.7% of the Moon’s mass (0.22% of Earth’s). Its surface area is 1.774443×10⁷ km², slightly larger than Russia or Antarctica (especially including winter sea ice), and its surface gravity is 0.063 g (compared to 1 g on Earth and 0.17 g on the Moon), giving it an escape velocity of 4,363.2 km/h (2,711.167 mph), more than twice the diameter and a dozen times the mass of Ceres. It is less massive than Eris, though it has a larger diameter (2,376.6 km vs. Eris’s ~2,326 km). With less than 0.2 lunar masses, Pluto is less massive than the terrestrial planets and seven moons (Ganymede, Titan, Callisto, Io, Moon, Europa, and Triton). The discovery of Charon in 1978 enabled accurate determination of the Pluto–Charon system’s mass via Newton’s version of Kepler’s third law, allowing more precise measurements of Pluto’s diameter and shape through occultation and adaptive optics. Size determinations were complicated by Pluto’s atmosphere and hydrocarbon haze; in March 2014, Lellouch, de Bergh et al. found methane mixing ratios consistent with a diameter greater than 2,360 km, with a best estimate of 2,368 km. New Horizons data from July 13, 2015, initially measured Pluto’s diameter at 2,370 km, revised to 2,372 km on July 24, and later to 2,374±8 km; radio occultation data from the New Horizons Radio Science Experiment (REX) confirmed the diameter as 2,376.6±3.2 km. Pluto has a tenuous atmosphere of nitrogen, methane, and carbon monoxide in equilibrium with surface ices, with a surface pressure of about 1 Pa (10 μbar)—one million to 100,000 times less than Earth’s. New Horizons data show that atmospheric density increases as Pluto moves away from the Sun, and the atmosphere likely remains gaseous throughout its orbit. Nitrogen escape is 10,000 times less than expected; Alan Stern suggests even a small temperature increase could exponentially raise atmospheric density, potentially leading to liquid nitrogen flow. Sublimation of the atmosphere cools Pluto’s surface; it has no or almost no troposphere, with only a thin, discontinuous boundary layer about 4 km thick and at 37±3 K. In July 2019, an occultation revealed a 20% drop in atmospheric pressure since 2016, confirmed in 2021 by data from a 2018 occultation showing a thinner atmosphere. Methane, a greenhouse gas, creates a temperature inversion, with the atmosphere averaging tens of degrees warmer than the surface, though upper atmosphere observations show temperatures of 70 K (vs. expected ~100 K). The atmosphere has about 20 regularly spaced haze layers up to 150 km high, likely formed by pressure waves from airflow over mountains. Pluto has five known natural satellites; Charon, discovered in 1978 by James Christy, is the largest and the only moon of Pluto believed to be in hydrostatic equilibrium, with its mass causing the Pluto–Charon barycenter to lie outside Pluto; beyond Charon are four smaller circumbinary moons.

Astronomers at the Southwest Research Institute confirmed data from a 2018 occultation event, which revealed that light from behind Pluto's disc appeared to diminish less gradually, indicating a thinning atmosphere. Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, is present in Pluto's atmosphere and causes a temperature inversion, making the average atmospheric temperature tens of degrees warmer than the surface, although New Horizons observations found the upper atmosphere to be significantly colder than expected—around 70 K instead of about 100 K. Pluto's atmosphere consists of roughly 20 regularly spaced haze layers extending up to 150 km in height, believed to form due to pressure waves generated by airflow over Pluto's mountains. Pluto has five known natural satellites: Charon, the largest and closest, first identified in 1978 by James Christy, which is the only moon of Pluto thought to be in hydrostatic equilibrium; Charon's mass causes the barycenter of the Pluto–Charon system to lie outside Pluto. Beyond Charon are four smaller circumbinary moons—Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra—discovered in 2012 (Styx), 2005 (Nix and Hydra), and 2011 (Kerberos), respectively. Their orbits are circular (eccentricity less than 0.006) and coplanar with Pluto's equator (inclination less than 1°), tilted approximately 120° relative to Pluto's orbital plane, and they all orbit within the inner 3% of the region where prograde orbits would be stable. The moons exhibit orbital resonances and near-resonances: when precession is considered, Styx, Nix, and Hydra have an exact 18:22:33 period ratio, and there is a sequence of approximate 3:4:5:6 ratios between Styx, Nix, Kerberos, Hydra and Charon, becoming more precise with greater distance. The Pluto–Charon system is unique in having its barycenter outside the primary body, with the Sun–Jupiter system being the only larger example and the Patroclus–Menoetius system being a smaller one; some astronomers refer to it as a double dwarf planet due to the similarity in size. Both bodies are tidally locked to each other, meaning they always show the same hemisphere to one another, a trait shared only with Eris and Dysnomia, and from any point on either body, the other remains in a fixed position in the sky or is always obscured. This tidal locking means each body's rotation period equals the system's orbital period around its barycenter. A collision between Pluto and a similar-sized body early in the Solar System is hypothesized to have formed the moons. In 2012, calculations suggested that 15810 Arawn could be a quasi-satellite of Pluto, remaining in such a configuration for about 350,000 years every two million years; New Horizons observations in 2015 refined Arawn's orbit and confirmed earlier data, though astronomers remain divided on whether Arawn should be classified as a quasi-satellite due to its primary orbital influence from Neptune. Early theories proposing Pluto as an escaped moon of Neptune were rejected because Pluto never approaches Neptune in its orbit. Pluto's true place in the Solar System became clear in 1992 when similar icy objects beyond Neptune were discovered, revealing a trans-Neptunian population; Pluto is the largest known member of the Kuiper belt, located between 30 and 50 AU from the Sun, and as of 2011, any remaining Pluto-sized objects are expected beyond 100 AU. Like other Kuiper belt objects, Pluto shares comet-like features, such as solar wind gradually eroding its surface; claims that Pluto would develop a tail if placed near Earth have been disputed due to its high escape velocity. Pluto may have formed from the aggregation of numerous comets and Kuiper belt objects. Though Pluto is the largest Kuiper belt object discovered, Neptune's moon Triton—larger than Pluto—is geologically and atmospherically similar and is believed to be a captured Kuiper belt object; Eris, similar in size to Pluto but more massive, is not considered a Kuiper belt object but rather part of the scattered disc. Pluto is thought to be a residual planetesimal from the original protoplanetary disc and its position results from Neptune's early migration outward, which disrupted the proto-Kuiper belt, captured some objects into orbit (like Triton), locked others into resonances, and scattered others into chaotic orbits; the scattered disc is thought to have formed from interactions with Neptune's migrating resonances. A 2004 model by Alessandro Morbidelli suggested Neptune's migration was triggered by a 1:2 resonance between Jupiter and Saturn, which pushed Uranus and Neptune into higher orbits and caused them to switch places, doubling Neptune's distance from the Sun, and this migration may have expelled objects from the proto-Kuiper belt, explaining the Late Heavy Bombardment and the origin of Jupiter trojans; Pluto may have had a near-circular orbit at about 33 AU before being perturbed into a resonant orbit. The Nice model requires about a thousand Pluto-sized bodies in the original planetesimal disk, including Triton and Eris. Pluto's great distance from Earth makes direct study difficult; its average visual magnitude is 15.1, brightening to 13.65 at perihelion, requiring a telescope with at least a 30 cm aperture to observe it, and it appears star-like without a visible disk due to its maximum angular diameter of 0.11". Early maps from the late 1980s were brightness maps derived from eclipses by Charon, measuring brightness changes during eclipses to infer surface features; Hubble Space Telescope images provided higher resolution, revealing details several hundred kilometers across, including polar regions and large bright spots, though these maps were later surpassed by New Horizons. The New Horizons spacecraft, launched in 2006, captured its first distant images of Pluto in late 2006 from about 4.2 billion kilometers away, confirming its ability to track distant targets, and used a Jupiter gravity assist in early 2007. It made its closest approach to Pluto on July 14, 2015, after a 3,462-day journey, with scientific observations beginning five months prior and continuing for at least a month afterward, using remote sensing instruments, spectroscopy, and radio science tools to study Pluto's geology, surface composition, and atmosphere. The final data from the encounter, totaling 50 billion bits or 6.25 gigabytes, was received on October 25, 2016. Since the flyby, scientists have called for an orbiter mission to fulfill new objectives, including mapping at 9.1 m per pixel, studying smaller moons, observing rotational changes, investigating a possible subsurface ocean, and creating topographic maps of permanently dark regions using laser pulses. Alan Stern has proposed a Cassini-style orbiter launched around 2030, the 100th anniversary of Pluto's discovery, using Charon's gravity for orbital adjustments and later leaving the system to study other Kuiper belt objects; a conceptual fusion-powered orbiter and lander based on the Princeton field-reversed configuration reactor has been funded by NASA's NIAC program. New Horizons imaged all of Pluto's northern hemisphere and equatorial regions down to about 30° South, while higher southern latitudes were only observed at low resolution from Earth; Hubble images from 1996 covered 85% of Pluto, showing large albedo features down to about 75° South, sufficient to reveal temperate-zone maculae, with slightly improved resolution later due to instrument upgrades. The equatorial region of the sub-Charon hemisphere was only imaged at low resolution due to the spacecraft's closest approach to the anti-Charon hemisphere. Some albedo variations in the southern latitudes were detectable via Charon-shine, and the south polar region appears darker than the north, though a high-albedo area in the southern hemisphere may represent a regional deposit of nitrogen or methane ice.
